notes.s: A letter to a friend who is gone, told as a winter that will not turn into spring.
notes.t: RM and Suga built this as the quiet closer of You Never Walk Alone, the February 2017 repackage of Wings, back when the group was still read in Korea as a loud hip-hop act. It is addressed to a friend who is simply not there any more, and it never says why. Much of the Korean audience hears the April 16 Sewol ferry disaster in it and points at the yellow coat and the counted days in the video; the company has never confirmed that reading, and the members have talked about it as a song about distance between friends. It returns to the Korean charts every spring and every winter, which makes it the rare idol single that behaves like a standard rather than a release.
k: Literally I want to see. Korean says missing a person as wanting to see them, so this is the ordinary way to say I miss you. The want-to-see frame is 보다 plus -고 싶다, which works on any verb: 가고 싶다 I want to go, 먹고 싶다 I want to eat.

설국열차 is the Korean title of Snowpiercer, the Bong Joon-ho film and the comic behind it, where the last of humanity circles a frozen planet on a train that can never stop. Calling his own heart the one train left turns the grief into something mechanical and unstoppable.

The spine of the chorus. -아/어야 means only if or must, so 기다려야 is must wait before anything else happens, and -(으)ㄹ까 is a question asked into the air rather than to a listener. Put them together for how long must I wait before it happens, a pattern that works with any verb.

눈꽃 is snow plus flower, the frost that sits on branches like blossom, and it falls through the whole song while nothing grows. 벚꽃, cherry blossom, arrives only in the last chorus. The song does its argument through which flower is on the branch, not through what the lyrics state.

vocab.note: For missing a place, a time or a thing. A person you miss gets 보고 싶다 instead

vocab.en: to be hateful, to be resented
vocab.note: The feeling toward someone you cannot stop caring about. 싫다 is plain dislike
Almost always said of time, fate or circumstance rather than of a person
Reaching contact, not arriving at a place, which is 도착하다
멀다 far plus -어지다 become. That ending turns any adjective into a change of state: 좋아지다 get better, 커지다 get bigger
Takes 밤 as its object, 밤을 새우다. Natives often misspell it 새다
For changing on its own. 바꾸다 is to change something deliberately
Used for erasing a person from memory as readily as for erasing writing

vocab.en: to ache with cold, to sting
vocab.note: For body parts and for a cold that hurts. 춥다 is for weather
널 보내다 is to let someone go emotionally
꽃을 피우다 with 피우다 is the causative, to make something bloom

vocab.en: to be eternal, to last forever
